title: HTTP1 to HTTP2 to HTTP3

segments.text: XDTP has been around since the 90s, how has it evolved over the years, what is the latest
development?
Let's take a look.
He is the progression of the XDTP version so far, from XDTP 1 to 1.1 to 2 and 2 now 3.
Let's look at each one more closely.
XDTP 1 came out in 1996, it is built on top of TCP, every request to the same server
requires a separate TCP connection.
XDTP 1.1 soon followed in 1997, it introduced a keep alive mechanism so a connection
could be reused for more than a single request.
The persistent connections we do is request latency, because the client does not need to
initiate expensive, TCP 3 way handshake for every request.
This worthwhile to note that XDTP 1.1 also added XDTP pipelining.
This in theory allows the client to send multiple requests before waiting for each response.
The response must be received in the same order as two requests.
It was tricky to implement correctly and many proxy servers in between did not handle pipelining
properly.
Its support was eventually removed from many web browsers.
XDTP 1.1 with pipelining also suffers from an issue called head of line blocking.
We've had a line blocking, subsequent requests on the same connection must wait for the
previous requests to complete.
If a request is blocked for any reason like packet loss, or subsequent requests on the
same connection are also impacted.
To keep loading performance at an acceptable level, browsers normally keep multiple TCP
connections to the same server and send requests to it in parallel.
XDTP 2 was published in 2015.
XDTP 2 introduces XDTP streams, where multiple streams of requests could be sent to the same
server on a single TCP connection.
Unlike XDTP 1.1 pipelining, each stream is independent of each other and it does not need
to be sent or received in order.
XDTP 2 solves the head of line blocking issue at the application layer, but the issues
still exist in the transport layer with TCP.
Also note that XDTP 2 introduces a push capability to allow servers to send updates to the
clients whenever new data is available with that requiring a client to pull.
XDTP 3 began as a draft in 2020 and has recently been published in June 2022.
It uses a new protocol called Quick, instead of TCP as the underlying transport protocol.
Quick is based on UTP, introduces streams as the first class citizen at the transport layer.
Quick streams share the same quick connections, so no additional handshix that required
to create new ones.
Quick stream at the liver independently.
In most cases, packet loss affecting one stream doesn't affect others.
This is how Quick eliminates the head of line blocking at the transport layer.
Quick is designed for mobile heavy internet usage.
People carrying smartphones, consonants, which from one network to another as they move
about their day, will TCP the hand of a one connection from one network to another is sluggish.
Quick implements a concept called connection ID, which allows connections to move between
IP addresses and network interfaces quickly and reliably.
Even though HTTP 3 has just been standardized, it is used by 25% of the websites and
supported by many web browsers.

Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
